articles.title: Why your physics project needs an anthropologist
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03623-wPicking a site for an observatory should be about more than science. Humanities scholars have a crucial role in responsible siting.
articles.content:
The TAMBO team assesses suitable observatory sites in the Andes Mountains of Peru.Credit: Jaco de Swart

It is uncommon for a social scientist to have a seat at a meeting about an astronomical observatory, let alone for them to jointly lead one. For one-quarter of attendees to be social-science scholars is almost unprecedented. But that’s exactly what happens at meetings about the Tau Air-shower Mountain-based Observatory (TAMBO), a proposed detector to be built in the Peruvian Andes to look for cosmic particles called tau neutrinos.

Space diplomacy: bridging the operating gaps between myriad missions

Tau neutrinos are elusive fundamental particles that are transmitted through space from black holes and other distant sources. When these particles interact with rocks on Earth, they can produce a shower of other, short-lived particles. The idea behind TAMBO is that if such a shower were emitted from one side of a deep canyon, it could be picked up by an array of 5,000 detectors on the other side (TAMBO collaboration. Nature Astron. 10, 947–951; 2026). The Andes Mountains of Peru contain many promising sites.

For those who live in the area, however, the case for TAMBO is less clear. The Andes are a sensitive ecological environment and home to Indigenous farming communities that consider the mountains sentient beings that are integral to their society. The area is also affected by legal and illegal mining, large-scale infrastructure projects and legacies of colonialism. This all leads to scepticism towards large projects that are developed by people from outside the area.

I am the co-principal investigator of the TAMBO collaboration, alongside Peruvian neutrino physicist Carlos Argüelles at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts. I lead the social-science and ‘responsible siting’ side of the project. Having received funding to build a proof-of-principle experiment called TAMBITO, we are searching for a potential location for the observatory.

Developing astronomers in Africa: ‘We wanted to create a discipline’

Since 2024, the TAMBO collaboration has built partnerships with 11 Peruvian institutions, which are involved in the design and development of the telescope. Scientific links are an important starting point, but they are not enough. No matter what their discovery potential is, big scientific experiments are not beneficial to everyone. For example, construction of the Thirty Meter Telescope has been stalled since 2015 because of protests triggered by objections to its planned site on Maunakea in Hawaii — a mountain that is sacred in Native Hawaiian culture.

To integrate environmental care into the project and build good relationships with the communities that might host the telescope, TAMBO brought in experts on the Andean region. In 2024, the collaboration held a workshop at Harvard’s Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study, at which scholars and policymakers discussed what equitable astrophysics in Peru would look like. This led to the formation of a responsible-siting team that includes geographers, sociologists and anthropologists who have worked in the Andes.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a significant interdisciplinary approach to scientific development that respects Indigenous communities and environmental concerns, promoting responsible siting of a major observatory project in Peru. This approach fosters equitable collaboration, cultural respect, and environmental care, benefiting local populations and setting a precedent for future scientific projects worldwide.
articles.personality_title: Scientists and anthropologists team up to build a respectful observatory in Peru
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Tau Air-shower Mountain-based Observatory (TAMBO) is a planned scientific project to detect rare cosmic particles called tau neutrinos in the Andes Mountains of Peru. These particles come from space and could help scientists understand the universe better.

**What happened** – Unlike many scientific projects, TAMBO includes social scientists like anthropologists and sociologists as part of its leadership. Since 2024, the project has partnered with 11 Peruvian institutions and formed a responsible-siting team. This team studies the best place to build the observatory while respecting the local Indigenous communities and the environment.

**Impact** – This approach is important because the Andes are home to Indigenous people who see the mountains as living beings and have concerns about outside projects. By involving social scientists and local partners, TAMBO aims to avoid conflicts like those seen with other observatories built on sacred lands. It shows how science can work together with culture and nature.

**What's next step** – TAMBO is currently searching for the best site to build the observatory with care for the environment and people. The project will continue to involve local communities and experts to make sure the observatory benefits science without harming the region.

**One-sentence takeaway** – TAMBO is creating a new model for science projects by combining physics with social science to build an observatory that respects Indigenous culture and nature in Peru.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des scientifiques et des anthropologues unissent leurs forces pour construire un observatoire respectueux au Pérou
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le Tau Air-shower Mountain-based Observatory (TAMBO) est un projet scientifique prévu pour détecter des particules cosmiques rares appelées neutrinos tau dans les montagnes des Andes au Pérou. Ces particules viennent de l’espace et pourraient aider les scientifiques à mieux comprendre l’univers.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Contrairement à beaucoup de projets scientifiques, TAMBO inclut des chercheurs en sciences sociales comme des anthropologues et des sociologues dans son équipe de direction. Depuis 2024, le projet a établi des partenariats avec 11 institutions péruviennes et formé une équipe chargée du choix responsable du site. Cette équipe étudie le meilleur endroit pour construire l’observatoire tout en respectant les communautés indigènes locales et l’environnement.

**Impact** – Cette approche est importante car les Andes abritent des peuples indigènes qui considèrent les montagnes comme des êtres vivants et s’inquiètent des projets extérieurs. En intégrant des scientifiques sociaux et des partenaires locaux, TAMBO vise à éviter des conflits comme ceux rencontrés avec d’autres observatoires construits sur des terres sacrées. Cela montre comment la science peut collaborer avec la culture et la nature.

**Prochaine étape** – TAMBO recherche actuellement le meilleur site pour construire l’observatoire en tenant compte de l’environnement et des habitants. Le projet continuera à impliquer les communautés locales et les experts pour s’assurer que l’observatoire profite à la science sans nuire à la région.

**Résumé en une phrase** – TAMBO crée un nouveau modèle de projets scientifiques en associant physique et sciences sociales pour construire un observatoire respectueux de la culture indigène et de la nature au Pérou.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos y antropólogos se unen para construir un observatorio respetuoso en Perú
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El Tau Air-shower Mountain-based Observatory (TAMBO) es un proyecto científico planeado para detectar partículas cósmicas raras llamadas neutrinos tau en las montañas de los Andes, en Perú. Estas partículas vienen del espacio y podrían ayudar a los científicos a entender mejor el universo.

**Qué pasó** – A diferencia de muchos proyectos científicos, TAMBO incluye científicos sociales como antropólogos y sociólogos en su equipo de liderazgo. Desde 2024, el proyecto ha formado alianzas con 11 instituciones peruanas y creado un equipo para elegir el sitio responsablemente. Este equipo estudia el mejor lugar para construir el observatorio respetando a las comunidades indígenas locales y al medio ambiente.

**Impacto** – Este enfoque es importante porque los Andes son hogar de pueblos indígenas que ven las montañas como seres vivos y tienen preocupaciones sobre proyectos externos. Al incluir científicos sociales y socios locales, TAMBO busca evitar conflictos como los que han ocurrido con otros observatorios en tierras sagradas. Esto muestra cómo la ciencia puede trabajar junto con la cultura y la naturaleza.

**Próximo paso** – TAMBO está buscando el mejor lugar para construir el observatorio cuidando el medio ambiente y a la gente. El proyecto seguirá involucrando a las comunidades locales y expertos para asegurar que el observatorio beneficie a la ciencia sin dañar la región.

**Resumen en una frase** – TAMBO está creando un nuevo modelo para proyectos científicos al combinar física con ciencias sociales para construir un observatorio que respete la cultura indígena y la naturaleza en Perú.
